workedExamples.title: Feasible region of a system is the OVERLAP (intersection), not the union

steps.prompt: A system has two inequalities: y ≥ x and y ≤ 4. We shade each one. What region answers the SYSTEM?
steps.reveal: A solution of the SYSTEM must make BOTH inequalities true at the same time. The answer is the OVERLAP — the region where the shading from y ≥ x and the shading from y ≤ 4 cover the SAME points. Where only one is shaded is not a solution.

steps.prompt: A student shades everything that satisfies y ≥ x OR y ≤ 4 and calls it the answer. Why is that wrong?
steps.reveal: That is the UNION (either-or), which is far too big. A system requires AND, not OR. The union counts points that satisfy only one inequality; those points fail the system. We keep only the intersection (the doubly-shaded slice).

steps.prompt: Test the point (1, 3). Is it in the feasible region?
steps.reveal: Check BOTH: y ≥ x → 3 ≥ 1 true. y ≤ 4 → 3 ≤ 4 true. Both hold, so (1, 3) is in the overlap and IS a solution of the system.

steps.prompt: Test the point (5, 3). Is it a solution?
steps.reveal: Check BOTH: y ≥ x → 3 ≥ 5 FALSE. y ≤ 4 → 3 ≤ 4 true. It satisfies only ONE inequality, so it is in the union but NOT in the overlap. It is NOT a solution of the system.

steps.prompt: State the rule in one sentence.
steps.reveal: The feasible region of a system of inequalities is the intersection — the overlap where ALL inequalities are satisfied at once; a point counts only if it passes every inequality, never just one.

workedExamples.title: Each boundary keeps its OWN style: dashed for strict < or >, solid for ≤ or ≥

steps.prompt: A system is y > 2x − 1 and y ≤ x + 3. Both lines get drawn. Do both boundaries look the same?
steps.reveal: No. Each boundary is styled by its OWN inequality sign. y > 2x − 1 uses a STRICT sign (>), so that boundary is DASHED. y ≤ x + 3 uses ≤ (allows equal), so that boundary is SOLID. A single system can mix one dashed and one solid line.

steps.prompt: Why is the boundary of y > 2x − 1 dashed?
steps.reveal: Strict inequalities (< or >) do NOT include the line itself — points exactly on the line make it 'equal,' which '>' forbids. We draw the line dashed to show those boundary points are excluded.

steps.prompt: Why is the boundary of y ≤ x + 3 solid?
steps.reveal: ≤ and ≥ INCLUDE equality, so points exactly on the line ARE solutions. We draw the line solid to show the boundary itself is part of the region.

steps.prompt: A student draws BOTH boundaries solid because it is one system. What is the error?
steps.reveal: Boundary style is per-inequality, not per-system. Matching both to the same style is a boundary-type mismatch. You must read each sign separately: > stays dashed, ≤ stays solid — even within the same system.

steps.prompt: State the rule in one sentence.
steps.reveal: Match each boundary to its own inequality: dashed for strict < or >, solid for ≤ or ≥ — so a system can legitimately show a mix of solid and dashed lines.
